reference.source: Smith & Tanagho's General Urology / Campbell-Walsh Urology
clinicalPearls: Urethritis is inflammation of the urethra presenting with urethral discharge, dysuria, and urethral itch or discomfort, most often sexually transmitted

It is broadly divided into gonococcal urethritis (Neisseria gonorrhoeae) and non-gonococcal urethritis, of which Chlamydia trachomatis is the leading cause, along with Mycoplasma genitalium and others

Gonococcal urethritis classically produces a profuse purulent discharge, whereas non-gonococcal urethritis tends to cause a scantier, more mucoid discharge, though overlap is common and co-infection frequent

Diagnosis rests on demonstrating urethral inflammation (urethral smear with leucocytes or a positive leucocyte esterase on first-void urine) together with nucleic acid amplification testing for the causative organisms
Management principles include empirical antibiotic therapy covering both gonococcal and chlamydial infection, guided by local resistance patterns, plus abstinence until treatment is complete
Partner notification, treatment of sexual contacts, and a full sexually transmitted infection screen (including HIV and syphilis) are essential components of care
Persistent or recurrent urethritis after treatment may reflect reinfection, non-adherence, or organisms such as Mycoplasma genitalium with antimicrobial resistance
Reactive arthritis (urethritis, conjunctivitis, arthritis) may follow chlamydial urethritis, particularly in HLA-B27-positive individuals
reference.pathophysiology: Urethritis is inflammation of the urethral mucosa, usually caused by sexually transmitted organisms ascending the urethra. Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis are the principal pathogens, with Mycoplasma genitalium, Trichomonas vaginalis, and other organisms also implicated. Infection provokes a neutrophilic inflammatory response in the urethral epithelium, producing discharge and dysuria. Non-infective urethritis can follow trauma or instrumentation. Untreated infection may ascend or spread, causing epididymo-orchitis, prostatitis, disseminated gonococcal infection, or, historically, inflammatory urethral stricture, and in women pelvic inflammatory disease.
additionalDifferentials: Cystitis or lower urinary tract infection
additionalInvestigations: First-void urine or urethral swab nucleic acid amplification testing for gonorrhoea and chlamydia
Urethral Gram-stain smear for leucocytes and Gram-negative intracellular diplococci
Culture and antimicrobial sensitivities for Neisseria gonorrhoeae given resistance concerns
Testing for Mycoplasma genitalium and Trichomonas where indicated
Full sexually transmitted infection screen including HIV and syphilis serology
Urinalysis to help exclude urinary tract infection
redFlags: Features of disseminated gonococcal infection (fever, skin lesions, arthritis)
Ascending infection causing epididymo-orchitis or prostatitis
Persistent or recurrent urethritis suggesting resistant organism or reinfection
Systemic sexually transmitted co-infection such as HIV requiring identification
Reactive arthritis with ocular or joint involvement
reference.prognosis: Uncomplicated urethritis usually resolves rapidly with appropriate antibiotics and partner treatment; outcomes are worsened by reinfection, non-adherence, resistant organisms, and complications such as epididymo-orchitis or reactive arthritis.
pitfalls: Treating for chlamydia alone and missing co-existing gonococcal infection (or vice versa)
Neglecting partner notification and treatment, leading to reinfection
Failing to perform a full STI screen including HIV and syphilis
Overlooking Mycoplasma genitalium in persistent non-gonococcal urethritis
Not counselling on abstinence until treatment and partner therapy are complete
management: Give empirical antimicrobial therapy covering both gonococcal and chlamydial infection, using intramuscular ceftriaxone for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and doxycycline for Chlamydia trachomatis, guided by local resistance patterns

Send gonococcal culture with sensitivities before treatment given rising cephalosporin resistance, and treat identified Mycoplasma genitalium (macrolide or moxifloxacin) or Trichomonas vaginalis (metronidazole) accordingly
Advise abstinence from sexual contact until the patient and partners have completed treatment
Arrange partner notification and epidemiological treatment of recent sexual contacts
Perform a full sexually transmitted infection screen including HIV and syphilis serology
Reassess persistent or recurrent symptoms for reinfection, resistance or non-gonococcal causes, and manage complications such as epididymo-orchitis or reactive arthritis
